1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4.name: Scotch Game
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4.background: Ercole del Rio was the first author to mention it, in 1750, and the name comes from a correspondence match between Edinburgh and London in 1824. It declined by 1900, and Garry Kasparov led its revival in the late twentieth century.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4.name: Scotch Game
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4.strategy: The normal capture. Black has no good way to hold the pawn on e5, so it is exchanged for White's d-pawn and the centre opens: White's pieces become active, Black's develop easily, and the game is level.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 Nxd4.name: Scotch Game: Lolli Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 Nxd4.background: Popular in the nineteenth century, it received five columns of analysis in Freeborough and Ranken's Chess Openings Ancient and Modern in 1896.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 Nxd4.strategy: Trades knights and lets White's queen settle on d4, where it cannot easily be chased away. Sound, but Black has spent time and a developed piece, and White's pieces are the more active.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 Nf6.strategy: Develops with an attack on e4, but 4.dxe5 Nxe4 5.Qe2 hits the knight and it must retreat. Material is level, yet White has gained time and the pawn on e5 cramps Black, so White has the more comfortable game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4.strategy: The main line: White recaptures at once and puts the knight on the central square with the queen behind it. The centre is open without any pawn given away, and Black has to decide how to challenge the knight.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4.name: Scotch Game: Scotch Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4.strategy: Leaves the pawn on d4 alone and develops the bishop with pressure on f7, trading a pawn for quick development. Black cannot keep the extra pawn for long, so the question is whether White's lead in time is worth the loose centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.c3.name: Scotch Game: Göring Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.c3.background: Howard Staunton played it in the 1840s, and the earliest game with it was probably played in 1843. Carl Theodor Göring introduced it into master play in 1872.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.c3.strategy: Offers a second pawn in the manner of the Danish Gambit: instead of recapturing, White opens lines for fast development and pressure on f7. Black can decline in the centre and equalise, so it is a risky, practical choice that makes Black find the right answers.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Bb5.name: Scotch Game: Relfsson Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Bb5.strategy: Attacks the knight on c6 but leaves the pawn on d4 where it is. White regains it after trading the bishop for the knight, which doubles Black's pawns but gives Black the two bishops. Sound, but it spends a tempo.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4 Nf6.strategy: Develops with a hit on e4 instead of clinging to the extra pawn: Black prefers piece activity to material. It is the most common reply, and White has to react to the threat on e4 at once, either with a central push or by giving up a second pawn for speed.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4 Bc5.name: Scotch Game: Haxo Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4 Bc5.strategy: Defends the pawn on d4 with the bishop and points it at f2, so Black holds the extra pawn for the moment. It cannot be kept for long, and Black will often hand it back for safe development rather than face White's fast play.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4 Bb4+.name: Scotch Game: Scotch Gambit, London Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4 Bb4+.strategy: Checks first, to use the d4 pawn's control of c3 before White can build a centre: after c3 Black may take a second pawn. White gets open lines and a lead in development for the pawns, so the line is sharp and riskier for Black.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4 Bb4+ 5.strategy: Hits the bishop with a pawn and gains a tempo, offering a second pawn. It takes the natural square from the queen's knight, but it forces Black to decide at once whether to take, and a lopsided fight for development follows.

Blocks the check with the bishop and offers a trade of the dark-squared bishops. White stays a pawn down and has no tempo-gaining follow-up, so Black keeps the pawn and can develop without being hurried.

Blocks the check with the queen's knight, which is then pinned to the king and shuts in both the c1-bishop and the queen. White is a pawn down and develops awkwardly, so the gambit gets little compensation.

Takes the second pawn: Black is two ahead but undeveloped, so White gets lines and time. The pawn on c3 attacks b2 and cramps the queenside, which White must deal with before the compensation is gone.

Declines the second pawn and tucks the bishop away, but it hands the initiative to White. After cxd4 White has a broad centre and the lead in development, with Qb3 adding pressure on b7 and f7, so Black has given the pawn back for nothing.
Keeps the bishop on the a7-g1 diagonal and guards d4 a second time, but cxd4 hits the bishop at once and it must move again. Black loses time and White regains the pawn with a broad centre.

Castles instead of recapturing: development is faster and the lines stay open. If Black grabs a third pawn, the bishop recaptures on b2 with the long diagonal pointing at g7, and White has paid material for time and activity.
Takes back with the b-pawn and attacks the bishop. White is still a pawn down, but gets pawns on c3 and e4 and a half-open d-file as compensation: the quieter, structural way to pay for the gambit.

Recaptures with the knight, which is at once pinned by the bishop on b4. If Black takes with check, White recaptures with the b-pawn and has traded a knight for the bishop, still a pawn down for the open lines.

Retreats the bishop to a safe square where it still eyes the c3 pawn, avoiding a trade of bishop for pawn. Black stays a pawn up but must finish development before White's centre and open lines come to bear.
Retreats to the kingside but walks into 7.Qd5, which attacks f7 with the bishop behind the queen; only the king guards the pawn, and Black cannot parry the threat without losing material.
Puts the bishop on the kingside diagonal, out of reach of the pawns for now. It blocks Black's own d-pawn, so Black must watch the centre while White's pieces and open lines come into play.
Grabs a third pawn. After Bxb2 the bishop eyes the unguarded g7 pawn and White is castled and ahead in development, so Black must defend with care. Playable, but greedier than the calm moves.

Holds the extra material and gets on with development: the pawn takes e5 away from White's e-pawn and frees the c8-bishop, so Black can make the king safe. White has to prove that open lines and a lead in development are worth the pawns, while the bishop on c4 keeps f7 under pressure.

Develops with a hit on e4, the most active way to hold the pawns. It invites a sharp fight in the open centre, where White's lead in development and the bishop on c4 aimed at f7 are the compensation, so Black has to bring the pieces out quickly and keep the king out of the line of fire.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4 Bc5 5..strategy: Castles first and offers the pawn on d4 for a lead in development, planning to play c3 later, when ...Bb4+ no longer wins a tempo. The positions that follow are sharp, with both kings exposed.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4 Bc5 5..name: Scotch Game: Scotch Gambit, Sarratt Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4 Bc5 5..background: Long considered inferior, perhaps because of the well-known game Meek-Morphy, Mobile 1855, it has since appeared in grandmaster play.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4 Bc5 5..strategy: Attacks f7 a second time while Black cannot yet castle. But a developed knight moves again with the queen still at home, so the line is thought premature, and Black defends with the g8-knight, after which White must work to keep the initiative.

Offers a second pawn for a broad centre, with a trap behind it: after 5...dxc3? 6.Bxf7+ Kxf7 7.Qd5+ the queen checks and attacks the bishop on c5, so White regains the material with a strong attack. Black's sound answer is to ignore the pawn and develop.

The standard defence: the knight develops, though from the rim, and guards f7, so the double attack is met without a king move. Black is ready to give material back at the right moment and keeps a solid position.
The natural developing move loses material: 6.Nxf7 forks the queen and the h8-rook, and the king cannot take the knight because the bishop on c4 guards it. Black loses at least the exchange.

Develops the knight to e7, where it does not guard f7: 6.Nxf7 forks the queen and the h8-rook, and the king cannot recapture because the bishop on c4 protects the knight. Black loses at least the exchange.

Sacrifices the knight to drag the king out: after the exchanges on f7 a queen check regains the material, and Black's king has lost castling and stands in the open. The position is level but double-edged.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4 Bc5 5..name: Scotch Game: Vitzthum Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4 Bc5 5..strategy: Adds the queen to the attack on f7, but ...Qe7 guards f7 a third time and attacks the knight on g5. The attack stalls, Black keeps the extra pawn and White has nothing to show for it.

Retreats the knight after it has only provoked ...Nh6, so White is still a pawn down with the initiative gone. Black keeps the d4 pawn, which is defended as often as it is attacked, and can castle with the bishop on c5 untroubled.
The natural recapture. White has given a knight for a pawn and must now open the king with the bishop check to win the material back. Material stays level, but Black loses castling.

Castles into a trap: 7.Nxd8 is a discovered check from the bishop on c4, so Black cannot take the knight at once and the queen is lost for a knight at best. The knight on f7 must be taken or the queen moved first.
Saves the queen but not the rook: 7.Nxh8 wins the exchange. Black can try to trap the knight on its corner square, but that costs time and White is not obliged to leave it there.
Opts for solidity: the pawn supports the bishop on c5 and shuts out the e5 thrust that 5...Nf6 would allow, and it frees the c8-bishop. Black keeps the extra pawn for now and goes for a sound set-up.
Develops with a hit on e4, but it allows White to push e5 with tempo. The resulting open game is double-edged and considered good for White, so the natural move is not the safest here.

Retreats along the same diagonal, so d4 stays defended twice and White cannot simply retake it with the knight. The bishop is safe from a later b4 there, but Black spends a tempo while White gets on with c3 and the lead in development.

Offers the pawn back for a broad centre: the c-pawn attacks d4, which is defended only by the bishop and the knight, so Black has to decide whether to hold it. White opens lines for the pieces and is ready to play for the initiative.
Hangs the knight to the pawn on d4: ...dxc3 wins a piece for a pawn, and White's lead in development is no compensation for a whole piece.

Defends e4 with the rook and keeps White's plans flexible, but it does not challenge d4, so Black can use the time to finish development. White's compensation has to come from piece pressure and the bishop's aim at f7 rather than from regaining the pawn quickly.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4 Bc5 5..name: Scotch Game: Scotch Gambit, Cochrane-Anderssen Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4 Bc5 5..strategy: Pins the knight on f3 to the queen, so that it cannot take on d4 without losing the queen, and Black can hold the pawn a little longer. It leads to sharp play with chances for both sides, with the bishop on c4 still pressing f7.

Develops with a hit on e4 and does not try to hold d4: after White retakes with the c-pawn, the bishop is attacked and retreats, so Black gives the extra pawn back for a sound development. The game becomes an even fight in which White has the bigger centre and Black a solid position.

Takes the second pawn, but 7.Nxc3 recaptures with a developing move and White's pieces come out with threats against the king. Black keeps the extra pawn at the price of a worse-developed position and has to defend with care.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.c3 d5.name: Scotch Game: Scotch Gambit, Göring Gambit Declined
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.c3 d5.strategy: Declines by striking in the centre at once: the pawn on d5 hits e4, and after the exchanges White is left with an isolated pawn on d4 against active black pieces. A strong way for Black to equalise.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.c3 dxc3.strategy: Accepts the gambit. Black wins a pawn, perhaps two, but must survive White's pressure on f7 and the open centre. With accurate defence Black can keep the material, so this is the principled test of the gambit.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.c3 Nf6.strategy: Develops with a hit on e4, but invites 5.e5, which kicks the knight away and gains space. Black must then find accurate defence to hold the balance: a playable middle way between the pawn grab and the central strike, but less direct than the pawn on d5.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.c3 dxc3 5..strategy: Takes the pawn back with a developing move, so the gambit costs White only one pawn. The knight aims at d5 and e4, and the bishop and queen can bear down on f7. Black's task is to get the king safe and consolidate the extra pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.c3 dxc3 5..name: Scotch Game: Göring Gambit, Double Pawn Sacrifice
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.c3 dxc3 5..strategy: Offers a second pawn for even faster development: the bishop eyes f7 at once, and White sidesteps Black's most testing reply to the single-pawn version. If Black takes both pawns, White must find a lasting attack on the king to justify the investment.
Retakes with the b-pawn: it keeps a pawn centre on c3 and e4 and opens the b-file, but it takes the natural square away from the b1 knight, and White is still a pawn down with little to show for it.

Develops with a threat to e4 and leaves the second pawn alone for now. The game usually transposes into the main lines of the gambit, but Black meets White's quick development with development of his own instead of with greed.

The most common reply: the pawn takes e5 away from White's e-pawn and frees the c8-bishop, and Black simply waits for White to retake on c3. Play then usually follows the one-pawn gambit with White's bishop already on c4, Black a pawn up and the game roughly balanced.

Takes the second pawn: after Bxb2 Black is two pawns up, but the bishop eyes g7 along the long diagonal and White is ahead in development. With the queen's knight already on c6, Black cannot safely strike back with ...d5, so it has to defend patiently: principled but risky.

Recaptures with a developing move, so White is again only one pawn down with the bishop already on its attacking diagonal. The knight eyes d5 and e4. The cost is that it can be pinned at once, because the d-pawn is gone.
Pushes the pawn to hit the knight and gain space, but ...d5 strikes the bishop at once and the attack stalls. Black keeps the extra pawn and the better game.
Retakes with the b-pawn, but nothing defends e4: ...Nxe4 wins a second pawn, and White's queenside structure is broken for no gain in development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.c3 dxc3 5..name: Scotch Game: Göring Gambit, Bardeleben Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.c3 dxc3 5..strategy: Pins the knight, the piece White's attack leans on, and threatens to trade it off. Because Black has not played ...d6, White can strike in the centre at once, so Black must be ready for a sharp, forcing fight rather than a quiet defence.

A solid reply: the pawn guards e5 and frees the c8-bishop, but it leaves White's knight on c3 unpinned. White's attack keeps its force, and the game becomes a complicated fight in which Black has the extra pawn and White the lead in development.

Covers f6 and prepares to castle, but it does not meet White's threat of e5 driving the knight away with gain of time. After the knight moves White's pieces come into the attack on f7 and Black can hardly hold the extra pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.c3 dxc3 5..name: Scotch Game: Göring Gambit, Main Line
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.c3 dxc3 5..strategy: Pins the knight on which White's whole attack rests and threatens to trade it off, taking away the jump to d5. The most critical reply: with calm development Black makes White's lead in development fall short of paying for the pawn.

A solid reply: the pawn guards e5, frees the c8 bishop and gives the knight on c6 a safe base, but it leaves White's knight unpinned. White's attack keeps its force, and the game becomes a complicated fight with roughly equal chances.

Develops the bishop with pressure on f2 and keeps the extra pawn, but it gives up the pin on the c3 knight that makes ...Bb4 the critical reply. White's pieces come out freely and the bishop on c4 soon starts to press on f7.
Hits e4, but 6.e5 gains time on the knight and cramps Black. Black can still keep the extra pawn with accurate play, but it is a harder road than the sound replies.

Brings the bishop to its natural attacking diagonal, aimed at f7, and prepares to bring the queen and the other knight into the attack on that point. The pressure on Black's weakest square is White's compensation for the pawn.

Develops with tempo by attacking the queen, with the f3 knight guarding the bishop. Black can answer by moving the queen or blocking with a pawn, so White wins a move but no more, and the bishop is not aimed at f7, the weak point the gambit is meant to attack.

Puts the queen on the diagonal to f7 and attacks b7, but the bishop on c8 guards b7 and Black can cover f7 with the queen or a piece, so the queen has used a tempo without winning anything. White is playing for pressure on f7 with no piece developed to help.

Pins the f3 knight to the queen and threatens to damage White's pawns by taking it, but it leaves f7 under fire. Once Qb3 attacks b7 as well, a hasty ...Bxf3 runs into Bxf7+, and after ...Kd7 Qe6 is mate.

Develops with a hit on e4 and prepares castling, the most natural way to hold the extra pawn. Black meets White's pressure on f7 with natural development; the position is double-edged and roughly balanced, with White's lead in development as the compensation.

Challenges the bishop that eyes f7 and offers a trade: after Bxe6 fxe6 White's most dangerous attacker is gone and the f-file opens for Black. The cost is a looser pawn shield and a queen swing to b3 hitting b7, so Black keeps the extra pawn but must defend accurately.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 Nxd4 4.Nxd4.strategy: Takes on d4 and invites ...exd4, after which the queen's recapture centralises it for free. The trade works in White's favour because the knight that would have chased the queen has been exchanged.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 Nxd4 4.Nxe5.strategy: Wins back the pawn by taking on e5 and leaves Black's knight on d4 without a defender, so Black must save it at once. White regains the pawn with the freer game, though Black can equalise with accurate play.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 Nxd4 4.Qxd4.strategy: Recaptures with the queen straight into the e5 pawn, which takes it: White loses the queen for a knight.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 Nxd4 4.Nxd4 exd4.strategy: The natural recapture, which restores material but leaves the d4 pawn attacked by the queen at once. Black must accept that White gets the more comfortable game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 Nxd4 4.Nxd4 Bc5.strategy: Piles up on the d4 knight but leaves it in place: White simply moves it away and stays a piece up for a pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 Nxd4 4.Nxd4 c5.strategy: Hits the knight with a pawn instead of recapturing it, but the knight just moves away and White stays a piece up for a pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 Nxd4 4.Nxd4 exd4.strategy: Takes the pawn with the queen, which stands centrally and cannot be chased away easily. White gets the more active position; Black is slightly passive but can hold with accurate play.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 Nxd4 4.Nxd4 exd4.name: Scotch Game: Napoleon Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 Nxd4 4.Nxd4 exd4.strategy: Develops with an eye on f7 and delays the recapture. The d4 pawn can still be taken later, but Black can now defend it with ...Qf6, so White has swapped a sure recapture for a lead in development.
Develops the knight to a square the d4 pawn attacks, so Black simply takes it, and after the recapture on c3 White is a knight down.
